quotes.text: "My dear Mr. Bennet,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "have you heard that Netherfield Park is let at last?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "But it is,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "for Mrs. Long has just been here, and she told me all about it."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Do not you want to know who has taken it?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "_You_ want to tell me, and I have no objection to hearing it."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Why, my dear, you must know, Mrs. Long says that Netherfield is taken by a young man of large fortune from the north of England; that he came down on Monday in a chaise and four to see the place, and was so much delighted with it that he agreed with Mr. Morris immediately; that he is to take possession before Michaelmas, and some of his servants are to be in the house by the end of next week."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "What is his name?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Bingley."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Is he married or single?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh!  single, my dear, to be sure!  A single man of large fortune; four or five thousand a year.  What a fine thing for our girls!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "How so?  how can it affect them?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "My dear Mr. Bennet,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "how can you be so tiresome!  You must know that I am thinking of his marrying one of them."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Is that his design in settling here?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Design!  nonsense, how can you talk so!  But it is very likely that he _may_ fall in love with one of them, and therefore you must visit him as soon as he comes."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I see no occasion for that.  You and the girls may go, or you may send them by themselves, which perhaps will be still better; for, as you are as handsome as any of them, Mr. Bingley might like you the best of the party."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "My dear, you flatter me.  I certainly _have_ had my share of beauty, but I do not pretend to be any thing extraordinary now. When a woman has five grown up daughters, she ought to give over thinking of her own beauty."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "In such cases, a woman has not often much beauty to think of."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "But, my dear, you must indeed go and see Mr. Bingley when he comes into the neighbourhood."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "It is more than I engage for, I assure you."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "But consider your daughters.  Only think what an establishment it would be for one of them.  Sir William and Lady Lucas are determined to go, merely on that account, for in general, you know they visit no new comers.  Indeed you must go, for it will be impossible for us to visit him, if you do not."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You are over-scrupulous, surely.  I dare say Mr. Bingley will be very glad to see you; and I will send a few lines by you to assure him of my hearty consent to his marrying which ever he chuses of the girls; though I must throw in a good word for my little Lizzy."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I desire you will do no such thing.  Lizzy is not a bit better than the others; and I am sure she is not half so handsome as Jane, nor half so good humoured as Lydia.  But you are always giving _her_ the preference."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "They have none of them much to recommend them,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "they are all silly and ignorant like other girls; but Lizzy has something more of quickness than her sisters."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Mr. Bennet, how can you abuse your own children in such way? You take delight in vexing me.  You have no compassion on my poor nerves."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You mistake me, my dear.  I have a high respect for your nerves.  They are my old friends.  I have heard you mention them with consideration these twenty years at least."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Ah!  you do not know what I suffer."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "But I hope you will get over it, and live to see many young men of four thousand a year come into the neighbourhood."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "It will be no use to us if twenty such should come, since you will not visit them."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Depend upon it, my dear, that when there are twenty I will visit them all."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I hope Mr. Bingley will like it, Lizzy."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "We are not in a way to know _what_ Mr. Bingley likes,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "since we are not to visit."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "But you forget, mama,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "that we shall meet him at the assemblies, and that Mrs. Long has promised to introduce him."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I do not believe Mrs. Long will do any such thing.  She has two nieces of her own.  She is a selfish, hypocritical woman, and I have no opinion of her."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "No more have I,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "and I am glad to find that you do not depend on her serving you."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Don't keep coughing so, Kitty, for heaven's sake!  Have a little compassion on my nerves.  You tear them to pieces."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Kitty has no discretion in her coughs,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "she times them ill."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I do not cough for my own amusement,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "When is your next ball to be, Lizzy?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "To-morrow fortnight."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Aye, so it is,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "and Mrs. Long does not come back till the day before; so it will be impossible for her to introduce him, for she will not know him herself."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Then, my dear, you may have the advantage of your friend, and introduce Mr. Bingley to _her_."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Impossible, Mr. Bennet, impossible, when I am not acquainted with him myself; how can you be so teazing?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I honour your circumspection.  A fortnight's acquaintance is certainly very little.  One cannot know what a man really is by the end of a fortnight.  But if we do not venture, somebody else will; and after all, Mrs. Long and her nieces must stand their chance; and therefore, as she will think it an act of kindness, if you decline the office, I will take it on myself."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Nonsense, nonsense!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "What can be the meaning of that emphatic exclamation?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Do you consider the forms of introduction, and the stress that is laid on them, as nonsense?  I cannot quite agree with you _there_.  What say you, Mary?  for you are a young lady of deep reflection I know, and read great books, and make extracts."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "While Mary is adjusting her ideas,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "let us return to Mr. Bingley."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I am sick of Mr. Bingley,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I am sorry to hear _that_; but why did not you tell me so before?  If I had known as much this morning, I certainly would not have called on him.  It is very unlucky; but as I have actually paid the visit, we cannot escape the acquaintance now."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "How good it was in you, my dear Mr. Bennet!  But I knew I should persuade you at last.  I was sure you loved our girls too well to neglect such an acquaintance.  Well, how pleased I am!  and it is such a good joke, too, that you should have gone this morning, and never said a word about it till now."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Now, Kitty, you may cough as much as you chuse,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "What an excellent father you have, girls,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I do not know how you will ever make him amends for his kindness; or me either, for that matter.  At our time of life, it is not so pleasant I can tell you, to be making new acquaintance every day; but for your sakes, we would do any thing.  Lydia, my love, though you _are_ the youngest, I dare say Mr. Bingley will dance with you at the next ball."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I am not afraid; for though I _am_ the youngest, I'm the tallest."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "If I can but see one of my daughters happily settled at Netherfield,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "and all the others equally well married, I shall have nothing to wish for."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Come, Darcy,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I must have you dance.  I hate to see you standing about by yourself in this stupid manner.  You had much better dance."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I certainly shall not.  You know how I detest it, unless I am particularly acquainted with my partner.  At such an assembly as this, it would be insupportable.  Your sisters are engaged, and there is not another woman in the room whom it would not be a punishment to me to stand up with."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I would not be so fastidious as you are,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "for a kingdom!  Upon my honour I never met with so many pleasant girls in my life, as I have this evening; and there are several of them, you see, uncommonly pretty."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "_You_ are dancing with the only handsome girl in the room,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh!  she is the most beautiful creature I ever beheld!  But there is one of her sisters sitting down just behind you, who is very pretty, and I dare say very agreeable.  Do let me ask my partner to introduce you."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Which do you mean?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "She is tolerable; but not handsome enough to tempt _me_; and I am in no humour at present to give consequence to young ladies who are slighted by other men.  You had better return to your partner and enjoy her smiles, for you are wasting your time with me."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh!  my dear Mr. Bennet,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "we have had a most delightful evening, a most excellent ball.  I wish you had been there.  Jane was so admired, nothing could be like it.  Every body said how well she looked; and Mr. Bingley thought her quite beautiful, and danced with her twice.  Only think of _that_ my dear; he actually danced with her twice; and she was the only creature in the room that he asked a second time.  First of all, he asked Miss Lucas.  I was so vexed to see him stand up with her; but, however, he did not admire her at all: indeed, nobody can, you know; and he seemed quite struck with Jane as she was going down the dance.  So, he enquired who she was, and got introduced, and asked her for the two next.  Then, the two third he danced with Miss King, and the two fourth with Maria Lucas, and the two fifth with Jane again, and the two sixth with Lizzy, and the Boulanger --"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "If he had had any compassion for _me_,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "he would not have danced half so much!  For God's sake, say no more of his partners.  Oh!  that he had sprained his ancle in the first dance!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh!  my dear,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I am quite delighted with him.  He is so excessively handsome!  and his sisters are charming women.  I never in my life saw any thing more elegant than their dresses.  I dare say the lace upon Mrs. Hurst's gown --"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "But I can assure you,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "that Lizzy does not lose much by not suiting _his_ fancy; for he is a most disagreeable, horrid man, not at all worth pleasing.  So high and so conceited that there was no enduring him!  He walked here, and he walked there, fancying himself so very great!  Not handsome enough to dance with!  I wish you had been there, my dear, to have given him one of your set downs.  I quite detest the man."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "He is just what a young man ought to be,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "sensible, good humoured, lively; and I never saw such happy manners! -- so much ease, with such perfect good breeding!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "He is also handsome,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "which a young man ought likewise to be, if he possibly can.  His character is thereby complete."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I was very much flattered by his asking me to dance a second time.  I did not expect such a compliment."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Did not you?  _I_ did for you.  But that is one great difference between us.  Compliments always take _you_ by surprise, and _me_ never.  What could be more natural than his asking you again?  He could not help seeing that you were about five times as pretty as every other woman in the room.  No thanks to his gallantry for that.  Well, he certainly is very agreeable, and I give you leave to like him.  You have liked many a stupider person."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Dear Lizzy!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh!  you are a great deal too apt, you know, to like people in general.  You never see a fault in any body.  All the world are good and agreeable in your eyes.  I never heard you speak ill of a human being in my life."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I would wish not to be hasty in censuring any one; but I always speak what I think."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I know you do; and it is _that_ which makes the wonder.  With _your_ good sense, to be honestly blind to the follies and nonsense of others!  Affectation of candour is common enough; -- one meets it every where.  But to be candid without ostentation or design -- to take the good of every body's character and make it still better, and say nothing of the bad -- belongs to you alone.  And so, you like this man's sisters too, do you?  Their manners are not equal to his."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Certainly not; at first.  But they are very pleasing women when you converse with them.  Miss Bingley is to live with her brother and keep his house; and I am much mistaken if we shall not find a very charming neighbour in her."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "_You_ began the evening well, Charlotte,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You were Mr. Bingley's first choice."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Yes; -- but he seemed to like his second better."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh! -- you mean Jane, I suppose -- because he danced with her twice.  To be sure that _did_ seem as if he admired her -- indeed I rather believe he _did_ -- I heard something about it -- but I hardly know what -- something about Mr. Robinson."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Perhaps you mean what I overheard between him and Mr. Robinson; did not I mention it to you?  Mr. Robinson's asking him how he liked our Meryton assemblies, and whether he did not think there were a great many pretty women in the room, and _which_ he thought the prettiest?  and his answering immediately to the last question -- "Oh!  the eldest Miss Bennet beyond a doubt, there cannot be two opinions on that point."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"

"Upon my word! -- Well, that was very decided indeed -- that does seem as if -- but, however, it may all come to nothing, you know."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "_My_ overhearings were more to the purpose than _yours_, Eliza,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Mr. Darcy is not so well worth listening to as his friend, is he? -- Poor Eliza! -- to be only just _tolerable_."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I beg you would not put it into Lizzy's head to be vexed by his ill-treatment; for he is such a disagreeable man that it would be quite a misfortune to be liked by him.  Mrs. Long told me last night that he sat close to her for half an hour without once opening his lips."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Are you quite sure, Ma'am? -- is not there a little mistake?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I certainly saw Mr. Darcy speaking to her."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Aye -- because she asked him at last how he liked Netherfield, and he could not help answering her; -- but she said he seemed very angry at being spoke to."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Miss Bingley told me,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "that he never speaks much unless among his intimate acquaintance.  With _them_ he is remarkably agreeable."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I do not believe a word of it, my dear.  If he had been so very agreeable, he would have talked to Mrs. Long.  But I can guess how it was; every body says that he is ate up with pride, and I dare say he had heard somehow that Mrs. Long does not keep a carriage, and had come to the ball in a hack chaise."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I do not mind his not talking to Mrs. Long,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "but I wish he had danced with Eliza."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Another time, Lizzy,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I would not dance with _him_, if I were you."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I believe, Ma'am, I may safely promise you _never_ to dance with him."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "His pride,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "does not offend _me_ so much as pride often does, because there is an excuse for it.  One cannot wonder that so very fine a young man, with family, fortune, every thing in his favour, should think highly of himself.  If I may so express it, he has a _right_ to be proud."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "That is very true,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "and I could easily forgive _his_ pride, if he had not mortified _mine_."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Pride,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "is a very common failing I believe.  By all that I have ever read, I am convinced that it is very common indeed, that human nature is particularly prone to it, and that there are very few of us who do not cherish a feeling of self-complacency on the score of some quality or other, real or imaginary.  Vanity and pride are different things, though the words are often used synonimously.  A person may be proud without being vain.  Pride relates more to our opinion of ourselves, vanity to what we would have others think of us."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "If I were as rich as Mr. Darcy,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I should not care how proud I was. I would keep a pack of foxhounds, and drink a bottle of wine every day."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Then you would drink a great deal more than you ought,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "and if I were to see you at it, I should take away your bottle directly."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "It may perhaps be pleasant,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "to be able to impose on the public in such a case; but it is sometimes a disadvantage to be so very guarded.  If a woman conceals her affection with the same skill from the object of it, she may lose the opportunity of fixing him; and it will then be but poor consolation to believe the world equally in the dark. There is so much of gratitude or vanity in almost every attachment, that it is not safe to leave any to itself.  We can all _begin_ freely -- a slight preference is natural enough; but there are very few of us who have heart enough to be really in love without encouragement.  In nine cases out of ten, a woman had better shew _more_ affection than she feels.  Bingley likes your sister undoubtedly; but he may never do more than like her, if she does not help him on."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "But she does help him on, as much as her nature will allow. If _I_ can perceive her regard for him, he must be a simpleton indeed not to discover it too."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Remember, Eliza, that he does not know Jane's disposition as you do."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "But if a woman is partial to a man, and does not endeavour to conceal it, he must find it out."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Perhaps he must, if he sees enough of her.  But though Bingley and Jane meet tolerably often, it is never for many hours together; and as they always see each other in large mixed parties, it is impossible that every moment should be employed in conversing together.  Jane should therefore make the most of every half hour in which she can command his attention.  When she is secure of him, there will be leisure for falling in love as much as she chuses."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Your plan is a good one,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "where nothing is in question but the desire of being well married; and if I were determined to get a rich husband, or any husband, I dare say I should adopt it.  But these are not Jane's feelings; she is not acting by design.  As yet, she cannot even be certain of the degree of her own regard, nor of its reasonableness.  She has known him only a fortnight.  She danced four dances with him at Meryton; she saw him one morning at his own house, and has since dined in company with him four times.  This is not quite enough to make her understand his character."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Not as you represent it.  Had she merely _dined_ with him, she might only have discovered whether he had a good appetite; but you must remember that four evenings have been also spent together -- and four evenings may do a great deal."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Yes; these four evenings have enabled them to ascertain that they both like Vingt-un better than Commerce; but with respect to any other leading characteristic, I do not imagine that much has been unfolded."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Well,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I wish Jane success with all my heart; and if she were married to him to-morrow, I should think she had as good a chance of happiness as if she were to be studying his character for a twelvemonth.  Happiness in marriage is entirely a matter of chance.  If the dispositions of the parties are ever so well known to each other, or ever so similar before-hand, it does not advance their felicity in the least.  They always contrive to grow sufficiently unlike afterwards to have their share of vexation; and it is better to know as little as possible of the defects of the person with whom you are to pass your life."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You make me laugh, Charlotte; but it is not sound.  You know it is not sound, and that you would never act in this way yourself."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "What does Mr. Darcy mean,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "by listening to my conversation with Colonel Forster?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "That is a question which Mr. Darcy only can answer."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "But if he does it any more, I shall certainly let him know that I see what he is about.  He has a very satirical eye, and if I do not begin by being impertinent myself, I shall soon grow afraid of him."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Did not you think, Mr. Darcy, that I expressed myself uncommonly well just now, when I was teazing Colonel Forster to give us a ball at Meryton?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "With great energy; -- but it is a subject which always makes a lady energetic."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You are severe on us."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "It will be _her_ turn soon to be teazed,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I am going to open the instrument, Eliza, and you know what follows."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You are a very strange creature by way of a friend! -- always wanting me to play and sing before any body and every body! -- If my vanity had taken a musical turn, you would have been invaluable, but as it is, I would really rather not sit down before those who must be in the habit of hearing the very best performers."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Very well; if it must be so, it must."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "There is a fine old saying, which every body here is of course familiar with -- "Keep your breath to cool your porridge,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"

Her performance was pleasing, though by no means capital. After a song or two, and before she could reply to the entreaties of several that she would sing again, she was eagerly succeeded at the instrument by her sister Mary, who having, in consequence of being the only plain one in the family, worked hard for knowledge and accomplishments, was always impatient for display.

Mary had neither genius nor taste; and though vanity had given her application, it had given her likewise a pedantic air and conceited manner, which would have injured a higher degree of excellence than she had reached.  Elizabeth, easy and unaffected, had been listened to with much more pleasure, though not playing half so well; and Mary, at the end of a long concerto, was glad to purchase praise and gratitude by Scotch and Irish airs, at the request of her younger sisters, who, with some of the Lucases and two or three officers, joined eagerly in dancing at one end of the room.

Mr. Darcy stood near them in silent indignation at such a mode of passing the evening, to the exclusion of all conversation, and was too much engrossed by his own thoughts to perceive that Sir William Lucas was his neighbour, till Sir William thus began.

"What a charming amusement for young people this is, Mr. Darcy! -- There is nothing like dancing after all. -- I consider it as one of the first refinements of polished societies."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Certainly, Sir; -- and it has the advantage also of being in vogue amongst the less polished societies of the world. -- Every savage can dance."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Your friend performs delightfully;"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "and I doubt not that you are an adept in the science yourself, Mr. Darcy."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You saw me dance at Meryton, I believe, Sir."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Yes, indeed, and received no inconsiderable pleasure from the sight.  Do you often dance at St. James's?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Never, sir."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Do you not think it would be a proper compliment to the place?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "It is a compliment which I never pay to any place, if I can avoid it."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You have a house in town, I conclude?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I had once some thoughts of fixing in town myself -- for I am fond of superior society; but I did not feel quite certain that the air of London would agree with Lady Lucas."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "My dear Miss Eliza, why are not you dancing? -- Mr. Darcy, you must allow me to present this young lady to you as a very desirable partner. -- You cannot refuse to dance, I am sure, when so much beauty is before you."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Indeed, Sir, I have not the least intention of dancing. -- I entreat you not to suppose that I moved this way in order to beg for a partner."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You excel so much in the dance, Miss Eliza, that it is cruel to deny me the happiness of seeing you; and though this gentleman dislikes the amusement in general, he can have no objection, I am sure, to oblige us for one half hour."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Mr. Darcy is all politeness,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "He is indeed -- but considering the inducement, my dear Miss Eliza, we cannot wonder at his complaisance; for who would object to such a partner?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I can guess the subject of your reverie."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I should imagine not."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You are considering how insupportable it would be to pass many evenings in this manner -- in such society; and indeed I am quite of your opinion.  I was never more annoyed!  The insipidity and yet the noise; the nothingness and yet the self-importance of all these people! -- What would I give to hear your strictures on them!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Your conjecture is totally wrong, I assure you.  My mind was more agreeably engaged.  I have been meditating on the very great pleasure which a pair of fine eyes in the face of a pretty woman can bestow."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Miss Elizabeth Bennet."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Miss Elizabeth Bennet!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I am all astonishment.  How long has she been such a favourite? -- and pray when am I to wish you joy?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "That is exactly the question which I expected you to ask. A lady's imagination is very rapid; it jumps from admiration to love, from love to matrimony, in a moment.  I knew you would be wishing me joy."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Nay, if you are so serious about it, I shall consider the matter as absolutely settled.  You will have a charming mother-in-law, indeed, and of course she will be always at Pemberley with you."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "From all that I can collect by your manner of talking, you must be two of the silliest girls in the country.  I have suspected it some time, but I am now convinced."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I am astonished, my dear,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "that you should be so ready to think your own children silly.  If I wished to think slightingly of any body's children, it should not be of my own, however."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "If my children are silly I must hope to be always sensible of it."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Yes -- but as it happens, they are all of them very clever."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "This is the only point, I flatter myself, on which we do not agree.  I had hoped that our sentiments coincided in every particular, but I must so far differ from you as to think our two youngest daughters uncommonly foolish."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "My dear Mr. Bennet, you must not expect such girls to have the sense of their father and mother. -- When they get to our age, I dare say they will not think about officers any more than we do.  I remember the time when I liked a red coat myself very well -- and indeed, so I do still at my heart; and if a smart young colonel, with five or six thousand a year, should want one of my girls, I shall not say nay to him; and I thought Colonel Forster looked very becoming the other night at Sir William's in his regimentals."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Mama,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "my aunt says that Colonel Forster and Captain Carter do not go so often to Miss Watson's as they did when they first came; she sees them now very often standing in Clarke's library."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Well, Jane, who is it from?  what is it about?  what does he say?  Well, Jane, make haste and tell us; make haste, my love."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "It is from Miss Bingley,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"My dear Friend,

IF you are not so compassionate as to dine to-day with Louisa and me, we shall be in danger of hating each other for the rest of our lives, for a whole day's te^te-a`-te^te between two women can never end without a quarrel.  Come as soon as you can on the receipt of this.  My brother and the gentlemen are to dine with the officers.  Yours ever,

CAROLINE BINGLEY."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "With the officers!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I wonder my aunt did not tell us of _that_."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Dining out,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "that is very unlucky."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Can I have the carriage?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "No, my dear, you had better go on horseback, because it seems likely to rain; and then you must stay all night."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "That would be a good scheme,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "if you were sure that they would not offer to send her home."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh!  but the gentlemen will have Mr. Bingley's chaise to go to Meryton; and the Hursts have no horses to theirs."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I had much rather go in the coach."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "But, my dear, your father cannot spare the horses, I am sure. They are wanted in the farm, Mr. Bennet, are not they?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "They are wanted in the farm much oftener than I can get them."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "But if you have got them to-day,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "my mother's purpose will be answered."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "This was a lucky idea of mine, indeed!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"My dearest Lizzy,

I FIND myself very unwell this morning, which, I suppose, is to be imputed to my getting wet through yesterday.  My kind friends will not hear of my returning home till I am better. They insist also on my seeing Mr. Jones -- therefore do not be alarmed if you should hear of his having been to me -- and excepting a sore throat and head-ache, there is not much the matter with me.

Yours, &c."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Well, my dear,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "if your daughter should have a dangerous fit of illness, if she should die, it would be a comfort to know that it was all in pursuit of Mr. Bingley, and under your orders."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh!  I am not at all afraid of her dying.  People do not die of little trifling colds.  She will be taken good care of.  As long is she stays there, it is all very well.  I would go and see her, if I could have the carriage."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "How can you be so silly,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "as to think of such a thing, in all this dirt!  You will not be fit to be seen when you get there."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I shall be very fit to see Jane -- which is all I want."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Is this a hint to me, Lizzy,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "to send for the horses?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "No, indeed.  I do not wish to avoid the walk.  The distance is nothing, when one has a motive; only three miles.  I shall be back by dinner."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I admire the activity of your benevolence,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "but every impulse of feeling should be guided by reason; and, in my opinion, exertion should always be in proportion to what is required."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "We will go as far as Meryton with you,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "If we make haste,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "perhaps we may see something of Captain Carter before he goes."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "She has nothing, in short, to recommend her, but being an excellent walker.  I shall never forget her appearance this morning.  She really looked almost wild."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "She did indeed, Louisa.  I could hardly keep my countenance. Very nonsensical to come at all!  Why must _she_ be scampering about the country, because her sister had a cold?  Her hair so untidy, so blowsy!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Yes, and her petticoat; I hope you saw her petticoat, six inches deep in mud, I am absolutely certain; and the gown which had been let down to hide it not doing its office."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Your picture may be very exact, Louisa,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "but this was all lost upon me.  I thought Miss Elizabeth Bennet looked remarkably well, when she came into the room this morning.  Her dirty petticoat quite escaped my notice."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "_You_ observed it, Mr. Darcy, I am sure,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "and I am inclined to think that you would not wish to see _your_ _sister_ make such an exhibition."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Certainly not."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "To walk three miles, or four miles, or five miles, or whatever it is, above her ancles in dirt, and alone, quite alone!  what could she mean by it?  It seems to me to shew an abominable sort of conceited independence, a most country-town indifference to decorum."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "It shews an affection for her sister that is very pleasing,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I am afraid, Mr. Darcy,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "that this adventure has rather affected your admiration of her fine eyes."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Not at all,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "they were brightened by the exercise."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I have an excessive regard for Jane Bennet, she is really a very sweet girl, and I wish with all my heart she were well settled.  But with such a father and mother, and such low connections, I am afraid there is no chance of it."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I think I have heard you say, that their uncle is an attorney in Meryton."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Yes; and they have another, who lives somewhere near Cheapside."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "That is capital,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "If they had uncles enough to fill _all_ Cheapside,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "it would not make them one jot less agreeable."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "But it must very materially lessen their chance of marrying men of any consideration in the world,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Do you prefer reading to cards?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "that is rather singular."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Miss Eliza Bennet,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "despises cards. She is a great reader and has no pleasure in anything else."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I deserve neither such praise nor such censure,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I am _not_ a great reader, and I have pleasure in many things."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "In nursing your sister I am sure you have pleasure,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "and I hope it will soon be increased by seeing her quite well."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "And I wish my collection were larger for your benefit and my own credit; but I am an idle fellow, and though I have not many, I have more than I ever look into."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I am astonished,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "that my father should have left so small a collection of books. -- What a delightful library you have at Pemberley, Mr. Darcy!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "It ought to be good,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "it has been the work of many generations."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "And then you have added so much to it yourself, you are always buying books."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I cannot comprehend the neglect of a family library in such days as these."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Neglect!  I am sure you neglect nothing that can add to the beauties of that noble place.  Charles, when you build _your_ house, I wish it may be half as delightful as Pemberley."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I wish it may."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "But I would really advise you to make your purchase in that neighbourhood, and take Pemberley for a kind of model.  There is not a finer county in England than Derbyshire."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "With all my heart; I will buy Pemberley itself if Darcy will sell it."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I am talking of possibilities, Charles."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Upon my word, Caroline, I should think it more possible to get Pemberley by purchase than by imitation."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Is Miss Darcy much grown since the spring?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "will she be as tall as I am?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I think she will.  She is now about Miss Elizabeth Bennet's height, or rather taller."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "How I long to see her again!  I never met with anybody who delighted me so much.  Such a countenance, such manners, and so extremely accomplished for her age!  Her performance on the piano-forte is exquisite."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "It is amazing to me,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "how young ladies can have patience to be so very accomplished as they all are."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "All young ladies accomplished!  My dear Charles, what do you mean?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Yes all of them, I think.  They all paint tables, cover skreens, and net purses.  I scarcely know any one who cannot do all this, and I am sure I never heard a young lady spoken of for the first time, without being informed that she was very accomplished."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Your list of the common extent of accomplishments,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "has too much truth.  The word is applied to many a woman who deserves it no otherwise than by netting a purse, or covering a skreen.  But I am very far from agreeing with you in your estimation of ladies in general.  I cannot boast of knowing more than half a dozen, in the whole range of my acquaintance, that are really accomplished."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Nor I, I am sure,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Then,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "you must comprehend a great deal in your idea of an accomplished women."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Yes; I do comprehend a great deal in it."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh!  certainly,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "no one can be really esteemed accomplished, who does not greatly surpass what is usually met with.  A woman must have a thorough knowledge of music, singing, drawing, dancing, and the modern languages, to deserve the word; and besides all this, she must possess a certain something in her air and manner of walking, the tone of her voice, her address and expressions, or the word will be but half deserved."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "All this she must possess,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "and to all this she must yet add something more substantial, in the improvement of her mind by extensive reading."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I am no longer surprised at your knowing _only_ six accomplished women.  I rather wonder now at your knowing _any_."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Are you so severe upon your own sex, as to doubt the possibility of all this?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "_I_ never saw such a woman, _I_ never saw such capacity, and taste, and application, and elegance, as you describe, united."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Eliza Bennet,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "is one of those young ladies who seek to recommend themselves to the other sex by undervaluing their own, and with many men, I dare say, it succeeds.  But, in my opinion, it is a paltry device, a very mean art."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Undoubtedly,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "there is meanness in _all_ the arts which ladies sometimes condescend to employ for captivation.  Whatever bears affinity to cunning is despicable."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Indeed I have, Sir,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "She is a great deal too ill to be moved.  Mr. Jones says we must not think of moving her.  We must trespass a little longer on your kindness."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Removed!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "It must not be thought of.  My sister, I am sure, will not hear of her removal."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You may depend upon it, Madam,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "that Miss Bennet shall receive every possible attention while she remains with us."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I am sure,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "if it was not for such good friends I do not know what would become of her, for she is very ill indeed, and suffers a vast deal, though with the greatest patience in the world -- which is always the way with her, for she has, without exception, the sweetest temper I ever met with.  I often tell my other girls they are nothing to _her_. You have a sweet room here, Mr. Bingley, and a charming prospect over that gravel walk.  I do not know a place in the country that is equal to Netherfield.  You will not think of quitting it in a hurry I hope, though you have but a short lease."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Whatever I do is done in a hurry,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "and therefore if I should resolve to quit Netherfield, I should probably be off in five minutes.  At present, however, I consider myself as quite fixed here."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "That is exactly what I should have supposed of you,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You begin to comprehend me, do you?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh!  yes -- I understand you perfectly."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I wish I might take this for a compliment; but to be so easily seen through I am afraid is pitiful."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "That is as it happens.  It does not necessarily follow that a deep, intricate character is more or less estimable than such a one as yours."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Lizzy,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "remember where you are, and do not run on in the wild manner that you are suffered to do at home."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I did not know before,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "that you were a studier of character.  It must be an amusing study."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Yes; but intricate characters are the _most_ amusing.  They have at least that advantage."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "The country,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "can in general supply but few subjects for such a study.  In a country neighbourhood you move in a very confined and unvarying society."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "But people themselves alter so much, that there is something new to be observed in them for ever."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Yes, indeed,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I assure you there is quite as much of _that_ going on in the country as in town."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I cannot see that London has any great advantage over the country for my part, except the shops and public places.  The country is a vast deal pleasanter, is not it, Mr. Bingley?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "When I am in the country,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I never wish to leave it; and when I am in town it is pretty much the same. They have each their advantages, and I can be equally happy in either."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Aye -- that is because you have the right disposition.  But that gentleman,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "seemed to think the country was nothing at all."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Indeed, Mama, you are mistaken,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You quite mistook Mr. Darcy.  He only meant that there were not such a variety of people to be met with in the country as in town, which you must acknowledge to be true."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Certainly, my dear, nobody said there were; but as to not meeting with many people in this neighbourhood, I believe there are few neighbourhoods larger.  I know we dine with four and twenty families."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Yes, she called yesterday with her father.  What an agreeable man Sir William is, Mr. Bingley -- is not he?  so much the man of fashion!  so genteel and so easy! -- He has always something to say to every body. -- _That_ is my idea of good breeding; and those persons who fancy themselves very important and never open their mouths, quite mistake the matter."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Did Charlotte dine with you?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "No, she would go home.  I fancy she was wanted about the mince pies.  For my part, Mr. Bingley, _I_ always keep servants that can do their own work; _my_ daughters are brought up differently.  But every body is to judge for themselves, and the Lucases are very good sort of girls, I assure you.  It is a pity they are not handsome!  Not that _I_ think Charlotte so _very_ plain -- but then she is our particular friend."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "She seems a very pleasant young woman,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh!  dear, yes; -- but you must own she is very plain.  Lady Lucas herself has often said so, and envied me Jane's beauty. I do not like to boast of my own child, but to be sure, Jane -- one does not often see any body better looking.  It is what every body says.  I do not trust my own partiality.  When she was only fifteen, there was a gentleman at my brother Gardiner's in town, so much in love with her, that my sister-in-law was sure he would make her an offer before we came away.  But however he did not.  Perhaps he thought her too young.  However, he wrote some verses on her, and very pretty they were."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "And so ended his affection,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "There has been many a one, I fancy, overcome in the same way. I wonder who first discovered the efficacy of poetry in driving away love!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I have been used to consider poetry as the _food_ of love,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Of a fine, stout, healthy love it may.  Every thing nourishes what is strong already.  But if it be only a slight, thin sort of inclination, I am convinced that one good sonnet will starve it entirely away."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I am perfectly ready, I assure you, to keep my engagement, and when your sister is recovered, you shall if you please, name the very day of the ball.  But you would not wish to be dancing while she is ill."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh!  yes -- it would be much better to wait till Jane was well, and by that time most likely Captain Carter would be at Meryton again.  And when you have given _your_ ball,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I shall insist on their giving one also.  I shall tell Colonel Forster it will be quite a shame if he does not."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "How delighted Miss Darcy will be to receive such a letter!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You write uncommonly fast."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You are mistaken.  I write rather slowly."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "How many letters you must have occasion to write in the course of the year!  Letters of business too!  How odious I should think them!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "It is fortunate, then, that they fall to my lot instead of to yours."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Pray tell your sister that I long to see her."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I have already told her so once, by your desire."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I am afraid you do not like your pen.  Let me mend it for you.  I mend pens remarkably well."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Thank you -- but I always mend my own."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "How can you contrive to write so even?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Tell your sister I am delighted to hear of her improvement on the harp, and pray let her know that I am quite in raptures with her beautiful little design for a table, and I think it infinitely superior to Miss Grantley's."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Will you give me leave to defer your raptures till I write again? -- At present I have not room to do them justice."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh!  it is of no consequence.  I shall see her in January. But do you always write such charming long letters to her, Mr. Darcy?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "They are generally long; but whether always charming, it is not for me to determine."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "It is a rule with me, that a person who can write a long letter, with ease, cannot write ill."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "That will not do for a compliment to Darcy, Caroline,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "because he does _not_ write with ease.  He studies too much for words of four syllables. -- Do not you, Darcy?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "My stile of writing is very different from yours."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Charles writes in the most careless way imaginable.  He leaves out half his words, and blots the rest."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "My ideas flow so rapidly that I have not time to express them -- by which means my letters sometimes convey no ideas at all to my correspondents."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Your humility, Mr. Bingley,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "must disarm reproof."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Nothing is more deceitful,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "than the appearance of humility.  It is often only carelessness of opinion, and sometimes an indirect boast."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "And which of the two do you call _my_ little recent piece of modesty?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "The indirect boast; -- for you are really proud of your defects in writing, because you consider them as proceeding from a rapidity of thought and carelessness of execution, which if not estimable, you think at least highly interesting.  The power of doing any thing with quickness is always much prized by the possessor, and often without any attention to the imperfection of the performance.  When you told Mrs. Bennet this morning that if you ever resolved on quitting Netherfield you should be gone in five minutes, you meant it to be a sort of panegyric, of compliment to yourself -- and yet what is there so very laudable in a precipitance which must leave very necessary business undone, and can be of no real advantage to yourself or any one else?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Nay,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "this is too much, to remember at night all the foolish things that were said in the morning. And yet, upon my honour, I believed what I said of myself to be true, and I believe it at this moment.  At least, therefore, I did not assume the character of needless precipitance merely to shew off before the ladies."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I dare say you believed it; but I am by no means convinced that you would be gone with such celerity. "

quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "To yield readily -- easily -- to the _persuasion_ of a friend is no merit with you."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "To yield without conviction is no compliment to the understanding of either."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

A regard for the requester would often make one readily yield to a request without waiting for arguments to reason one into it.  I am not particularly speaking of such a case as you have supposed about Mr. Bingley.  We may as well wait, perhaps, till the circumstance occurs, before we discuss the discretion of his behaviour thereupon.  But in general and ordinary cases between friend and friend, where one of them is desired by the other to change a resolution of no very great moment, should you think ill of that person for complying with the desire, without waiting to be argued into it?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Will it not be advisable, before we proceed on this subject, to arrange with rather more precision the degree of importance which is to appertain to this request, as well as the degree of intimacy subsisting between the parties?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "By all means,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Let us hear all the particulars, not forgetting their comparative height and size; for that will have more weight in the argument, Miss Bennet, than you may be aware of.  I assure you that if Darcy were not such a great tall fellow, in comparison with myself, I should not pay him half so much deference.  I declare I do not know a more aweful object than Darcy, on particular occasions, and in particular places; at his own house especially, and of a Sunday evening when he has nothing to do."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I see your design, Bingley,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You dislike an argument, and want to silence this."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Perhaps I do.  Arguments are too much like disputes.  If you and Miss Bennet will defer yours till I am out of the room, I shall be very thankful; and then you may say whatever you like of me."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "What you ask,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "is no sacrifice on my side; and Mr. Darcy had much better finish his letter."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Do not you feel a great inclination, Miss Bennet, to seize such an opportunity of dancing a reel?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I heard you before; but I could not immediately determine what to say in reply.  You wanted me, I know, to say "Yes,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"

"Indeed I do not dare."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I hope,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "you will give your mother-in-law a few hints, when this desirable event takes place, as to the advantage of holding her tongue; and if you can compass it, do cure the younger girls of running after the officers. -- And, if I may mention so delicate a subject, endeavour to check that little something, bordering on conceit and impertinence, which your lady possesses."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Have you any thing else to propose for my domestic felicity?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh!  yes. -- Do let the portraits of your uncle and aunt Philips be placed in the gallery at Pemberley.  Put them next to your great uncle, the judge.  They are in the same profession, you know; only in different lines.  As for your Elizabeth's picture, you must not attempt to have it taken, for what painter could do justice to those beautiful eyes?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "It would not be easy, indeed, to catch their expression, but their colour and shape, and the eye-lashes, so remarkably fine, might be copied."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I did not know that you intended to walk,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You used us abominably ill,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "in running away without telling us that you were coming out."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "This walk is not wide enough for our party.  We had better go into the avenue."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "No, no; stay where you are. -- You are charmingly group'd, and appear to uncommon advantage.  The picturesque would be spoilt by admitting a fourth.  Good bye."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "very glad;"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "How pleasant it is to spend an evening in this way!  I declare after all there is no enjoyment like reading!  How much sooner one tires of any thing than of a book! -- When I have a house of my own, I shall be miserable if I have not an excellent library."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "By the bye, Charles, are you really serious in meditating a dance at Netherfield? -- I would advise you, before you determine on it, to consult the wishes of the present party; I am much mistaken if there are not some among us to whom a ball would be rather a punishment than a pleasure."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "If you mean Darcy,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "he may go to bed, if he chuses, before it begins -- but as for the ball, it is quite a settled thing; and as soon as Nicholls has made white soup enough I shall send round my cards."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I should like balls infinitely better,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "if they were carried on in a different manner; but there is something insufferably tedious in the usual process of such a meeting.  It would surely be much more rational if conversation instead of dancing made the order of the day."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Much more rational, my dear Caroline, I dare say, but it would not be near so much like a ball."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Miss Eliza Bennet, let me persuade you to follow my example, and take a turn about the room. -- I assure you it is very refreshing after sitting so long in one attitude."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "What could he mean?  she was dying to know what could be his meaning"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Not at all,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "but depend upon it, he means to be severe on us, and our surest way of disappointing him will be to ask nothing about it."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I have not the smallest objection to explaining them,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You either chuse this method of passing the evening because you are in each other's confidence, and have secret affairs to discuss, or because you are conscious that your figures appear to the greatest advantage in walking; -- if the first, I should be completely in your way; -- and if the second, I can admire you much better as I sit by the fire."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh!  shocking!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I never heard any thing so abominable.  How shall we punish him for such a speech?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Nothing so easy, if you have but the inclination,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "We can all plague and punish one another.  Teaze him -- laugh at him. -- Intimate as you are, you must know how it is to be done."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "But upon my honour I do _not_.  I do assure you that my intimacy has not yet taught me _that_.  Teaze calmness of temper and presence of mind!  No, no -- I feel he may defy us there.  And as to laughter, we will not expose ourselves, if you please, by attempting to laugh without a subject. Mr. Darcy may hug himself."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Mr. Darcy is not to be laughed at!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "That is an uncommon advantage, and uncommon I hope it will continue, for it would be a great loss to _me_ to have many such acquaintance.  I dearly love a laugh."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Miss Bingley,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "has given me credit for more than can be.  The wisest and the best of men, nay, the wisest and best of their actions, may be rendered ridiculous by a person whose first object in life is a joke."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Certainly,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "there are such people, but I hope I am not one of _them_.  I hope I never ridicule what is wise or good.  Follies and nonsense, whims and inconsistencies _do_ divert me, I own, and I laugh at them whenever I can. -- But these, I suppose, are precisely what you are without."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Perhaps that is not possible for any one.  But it has been the study of my life to avoid those weaknesses which often expose a strong understanding to ridicule."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Such as vanity and pride."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Yes, vanity is a weakness indeed.  But pride -- where there is a real superiority of mind, pride will be always under good regulation."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Your examination of Mr. Darcy is over, I presume,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "and pray what is the result?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I am perfectly convinced by it that Mr. Darcy has no defect. He owns it himself without disguise."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "No"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I have made no such pretension.  I have faults enough, but they are not, I hope, of understanding.  My temper I dare not vouch for. -- It is I believe too little yielding -- certainly too little for the convenience of the world.  I cannot forget the follies and vices of others so soon as I ought, nor their offences against myself.  My feelings are not puffed about with every attempt to move them.  My temper would perhaps be called resentful. -- My good opinion once lost is lost for ever."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "_That_ is a failing indeed!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Implacable resentment _is_ a shade in a character.  But you have chosen your fault well. -- I really cannot _laugh_ at it; you are safe from me."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "There is, I believe, in every disposition a tendency to some particular evil, a natural defect, which not even the best education can overcome."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "And _your_ defect is a propensity to hate every body."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "And yours,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "is wilfully to misunderstand them."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Do let us have a little music,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Louisa, you will not mind my waking Mr. Hurst."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I HOPE my dear,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "that you have ordered a good dinner to-day, because I have reason to expect an addition to our family party."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Who do you mean, my dear?  I know of nobody that is coming, I am sure, unless Charlotte Lucas should happen to call in, and I hope _my_ dinners are good enough for her.  I do not believe she often sees such at home."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "The person of whom I speak, is a gentleman and a stranger."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "A gentleman and a stranger! It is Mr. Bingley, I am sure.  Why Jane -- you never dropt a word of this; you sly thing!  Well, I am sure I shall be extremely glad to see Mr. Bingley. -- But -- good lord!  how unlucky!  there is not a bit of fish to be got to-day.  Lydia, my love, ring the bell.  I must speak to Hill, this moment."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "It is _not_ Mr. Bingley,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "it is a person whom I never saw in the whole course of my life."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "About a month ago I received this letter, and about a fortnight ago I answered it, for I thought it a case of some delicacy, and requiring early attention.  It is from my cousin, Mr. Collins, who, when I am dead, may turn you all out of this house as soon as he pleases."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Oh!  my dear,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I cannot bear to hear that mentioned.  Pray do not talk of that odious man.  I do think it is the hardest thing in the world that your estate should be entailed away from your own children; and I am sure if I had been you, I should have tried long ago to do something or other about it."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "It certainly is a most iniquitous affair,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "and nothing can clear Mr. Collins from the guilt of inheriting Longbourn.  But if you will listen to his letter, you may perhaps be a little softened by his manner of expressing himself."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "No, that I am sure I shall not; and I think it was very impertinent of him to write to you at all, and very hypocritical.  I hate such false friends.  Why could not he keep on quarrelling with you, as his father did before him?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Why, indeed, he does seem to have had some filial scruples on that head, as you will hear."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"Hunsford, near Westerham, Kent,

15th October.

DEAR SIR,

THE disagreement subsisting between yourself and my late honoured father always gave me much uneasiness, and since I have had the misfortune to lose him I have frequently wished to heal the breach; but for some time I was kept back by my own doubts, fearing lest it might seem disrespectful to his memory for me to be on good terms with any one with whom it had always pleased him to be at variance."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "There, Mrs. Bennet."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text:
"My mind however is now made up on the subject, for having received ordination at Easter, I have been so fortunate as to be distinguished by the patronage of the Right Honourable Lady Catherine de Bourgh, widow of Sir Lewis de Bourgh, whose bounty and beneficence has preferred me to the valuable rectory of this parish, where it shall be my earnest endeavour to demean myself with grateful respect towards her Ladyship, and be ever ready to perform those rites and ceremonies which are instituted by the Church of England.  As a clergyman, moreover, I feel it my duty to promote and establish the blessing of peace in all families within the reach of my influence; and on these grounds I flatter myself that my present overtures of good-will are highly commendable, and that the circumstance of my being next in the entail of Longbourn estate will be kindly overlooked on your side, and not lead you to reject the offered olive branch.  I cannot be otherwise than concerned at being the means of injuring your amiable daughters, and beg leave to apologise for it, as well as to assure you of my readiness to make them every possible amends, -- but of this hereafter.  If you should have no objection to receive me into your house, I propose myself the satisfaction of waiting on you and your family, Monday, November 18th, by four o'clock, and shall probably trespass on your hospitality till the Saturday se'nnight following, which I can do without any inconvenience, as Lady Catherine is far from objecting to my occasional absence on a Sunday, provided that some other clergyman is engaged to do the duty of the day.  I remain, dear sir, with respectful compliments to your lady and daughters, your well-wisher and friend,

WILLIAM COLLINS."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "At four o'clock, therefore, we may expect this peacemaking gentleman,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "He seems to be a most conscientious and polite young man, upon my word; and I doubt not will prove a valuable acquaintance, especially if Lady Catherine should be so indulgent as to let him come to us again."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "There is some sense in what he says about the girls however; and if he is disposed to make them any amends, I shall not be the person to discourage him."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Though it is difficult,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "to guess in what way he can mean to make us the atonement he thinks our due, the wish is certainly to his credit."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "He must be an oddity, I think,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I cannot make him out. -- There is something very pompous in his stile. -- And what can he mean by apologizing for being next in the entail? -- We cannot suppose he would help it, if he could. -- Can he be a sensible man, sir?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "No, my dear; I think not.  I have great hopes of finding him quite the reverse.  There is a mixture of servility and self-importance in his letter, which promises well.  I am impatient to see him."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "In point of composition,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "his letter does not seem defective.  The idea of the olive branch perhaps is not wholly new, yet I think it is well expressed."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You are very kind, sir, I am sure; and I wish with all my heart it may prove so; for else they will be destitute enough. Things are settled so oddly."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You allude, perhaps, to the entail of this estate."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Ah!  sir, I do indeed.  It is a grievous affair to my poor girls, you must confess.  Not that I mean to find fault with _you_, for such things, I know, are all chance in this world. There is no knowing how estates will go when once they come to be entailed."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I am very sensible, madam, of the hardship to my fair cousins, -- and could say much on the subject, but that I am cautious of appearing forward and precipitate.  But I can assure the young ladies that I come prepared to admire them. At present I will not say more, but perhaps when we are better acquainted --"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "That is all very proper and civil I am sure,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "and I dare say she is a very agreeable woman. It is a pity that great ladies in general are not more like her.  Does she live near you, sir?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "The garden in which stands my humble abode is separated only by a lane from Rosings Park, her ladyship's residence."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I think you said she was a widow, sir?  has she any family?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "She has one only daughter, the heiress of Rosings, and of very extensive property."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Ah!"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "then she is better off than many girls.  And what sort of young lady is she?  is she handsome?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "She is a most charming young lady indeed.  Lady Catherine herself says that in point of true beauty, Miss De Bourgh is far superior to the handsomest of her sex; because there is that in her features which marks the young woman of distinguished birth.  She is unfortunately of a sickly constitution, which has prevented her making that progress in many accomplishments which she could not otherwise have failed of; as I am informed by the lady who superintended her education, and who still resides with them.  But she is perfectly amiable, and often condescends to drive by my humble abode in her little phaeton and ponies."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Has she been presented?  I do not remember her name among the ladies at court."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Her indifferent state of health unhappily prevents her being in town; and by that means, as I told Lady Catherine myself one day, has deprived the British court of its brightest ornament. Her ladyship seemed pleased with the idea, and you may imagine that I am happy on every occasion to offer those little delicate compliments which are always acceptable to ladies. I have more than once observed to Lady Catherine that her charming daughter seemed born to be a duchess, and that the most elevated rank, instead of giving her consequence, would be adorned by her. -- These are the kind of little things which please her ladyship, and it is a sort of attention which I conceive myself peculiarly bound to pay."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You judge very properly,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "and it is happy for you that you possess the talent of flattering with delicacy.  May I ask whether these pleasing attentions proceed from the impulse of the moment, or are the result of previous study?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "They arise chiefly from what is passing at the time, and though I sometimes amuse myself with suggesting and arranging such little elegant compliments as may be adapted to ordinary occasions, I always wish to give them as unstudied an air as possible."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Do you know, mama, that my uncle Philips talks of turning away Richard, and if he does, Colonel Forster will hire him. My aunt told me so herself on Saturday.  I shall walk to Meryton to-morrow to hear more about it, and to ask when Mr. Denny comes back from town."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I have often observed how little young ladies are interested by books of a serious stamp, though written solely for their benefit.  It amazes me, I confess; -- for certainly, there can be nothing so advantageous to them as instruction.  But I will no longer importune my young cousin."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "As to her _younger_ daughters she could not take upon her to say -- she could not positively answer -- but she did not _know_ of any prepossession; -- her _eldest_ daughter, she must just mention -- she felt it incumbent on her to hint, was likely to be very soon engaged."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "stupid, disagreeable fellows."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I know little of the game, at present,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "but I shall be glad to improve myself, for in my situation of life --"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "About a month,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "He is a man of very large property in Derbyshire, I understand."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "Yes,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "his estate there is a noble one. A clear ten thousand per annum.  You could not have met with a person more capable of giving you certain information on that head than myself -- for I have been connected with his family in a particular manner from my infancy."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "You may well be surprised, Miss Bennet, at such an assertion, after seeing, as you probably might, the very cold manner of our meeting yesterday. -- Are you much acquainted with Mr. Darcy?"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "As much as I ever wish to be,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I have spent four days in the same house with him, and I think him very disagreeable."
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "I have no right to give _my_ opinion,"
quotes.speaker: Unknown

quotes.text: "as to his being agreeable or otherwise.  I am not qualified to form one.  I have known him too long and to well to be a fair judge. It is impossible for _me_ to be impartial.  But I believe your opinion of him would in general astonish -- and perhaps you would not express it quite so strongly anywhere else. -- Here you are in your own family."
quotes.speaker: Unknown
